newsitem.title: RUSSIA: NATO-Russia talks to continue next week.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia talks to continue next week.

text.p: Fresh talks to minimise Russia's objections to NATO expansion will be held in Moscow next week and could help pave the way for President Boris Yeltsin to attend a summit at which the Western defence alliance will open the door to new members.
Moscow had previously ruled out Yeltsin's participation in NATO's Madrid summit in July where Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to receive invitations to join the alliance.

But Deputy Russian Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov said on Wednesday that Yeltsin had told visiting Spanish King Juan Carlos, who said he would be glad to welcome the Kremlin leader in Madrid, that he might go.
"President Yeltsin replied that the issue would be considered, taking into account all factors," Ivanov told reporters without elaborating.

Moscow says nothing will make it drop its objections to the expansion, but it wants to minimise what it sees as a threat to its own and European security by signing a document defining Russian-NATO relations into the 21st century.
Yeltsin has said he wants to sign the document in Paris on May 27 and there have been intensive talks to seek a formula acceptable to both sides.

"As you know, yesterday there were expansive and detailed negotiations between Yevgeny Primakov, the Russian foreign minister, and Javier Solana, secretary-general of NATO, in Luxembourg," the Russian deputy minister said.
"Next week these talks will be continued in Moscow."
Primakov said later during an official visit to Luxembourg that Solana would arrive in Moscow on May 13.
Echoing a new conciliatory line coming from Moscow, Ivanov said both sides agreed that they should minimise the negative consequences of the expansion.
Yeltsin, in an interview with the Krasnaya Zvezda newspaper published on Wednesday, appeared to be preparing Russian public opinion for a compromise on the NATO issue.
But he still faces continued strong opposition from communists and nationalists, who said they would picket in front of NATO-country embassies in Moscow on Thursday.

Russia has been demanding strict curbs on any military activities in any new NATO member states, but the Western alliance says such demands are out of the question because such issues are a matter of national sovereignty.
"As you understand this topic is very delicate. Negotiations are very difficult," Ivanov said.
